newsitem.title: UK: Transco to sell 100 mn therms of natgas into U.K.
newsitem.headline: Transco to sell 100 mn therms of natgas into U.K.

text.p: Transco, the pipeline, transport and storage arm of BG plc, said it will sell three TeraWatt hours (TWh) or some 102 million therms of natural gas into the U.K. market by the end of May as its policy of holding "balancing margins" of gas in storage comes to an end.
Mark Sutton, manager of Commmercial Operations at Transco wrote to industry regulator Ofgas and gas shippers on Friday, outlining its decision.
Many in the industry expect it to put downward pressure on prices.
"The speculation is that it will," said one Transco source. "In theory such a big volume should depress prices. It's hard to see any other realistic scenario," he added.
But others said that the market has already discounted the effect, as dealers had already anticipated balancing margins would come to an end at the end of the winter.
Transco has a total available storage space of 37 TWh, so offering three TWh by tender represents over eight percent of all potential storage space.
Transco currently holds three different types of gas in storage. The first, Operating Margins gas, is booked to meet extra demand in case of incidents such as pipeline breaks or offshore failures.

The second, Top Up gas, is designed to meet extreme demand represented by the 1-in-20 peak day (a cold day of such severity that it might occur once every twenty years) or the 1-in-50 peak winter (a winter that would only be expected to occur once every fifty years).

To assess the volume required for this, Transco looks at the volume of gas booked into storage by other shippers, makes its own supply and demand forecasts, and books as much gas into its top-up account to meet exceptional demand.
As the storage year starts in April, Transco is still assessing storage requirements from other shippers and has yet to announce what volume it will book in this category.

Balancing Margins gas is the third type of gas held. It was introduced when the Network Code, the rule book governing gas trade in Britain and use of the Transco-operated pipeline system, was introduced.

Because of fears that, in the first winter under the Network Code, shippers may go out of balance and the flexibility mechanism - specifically designed to correct imbalances "within the day" - may not be sufficiently responsive, balancing margins were introduced to make sure there was reserve gas in storage.
But Transco has now taken the view that the flexibility mechanism is working adequately, and so has decided to sell the balancing margins.
Sutton said on Monday that the Network Code requires Transco to conduct a tender for each storage facility, inviting users to purchase that gas in storage.
Buyers will then have to ensure they have storage capacity of their own to allow the sale to consist of a simple transfer of ownership within the storage unit.
Tenders to sell the gas will be issued by mid-May, with the tender closing before the end of May.
If there is insufficient interest to buy all the gas in storage, Transco is required to dispose of the gas by taking "other reasonable means."
Sutton said that this would probably mean moving the gas out of storage and selling it on the spot market at the National Balancing Point.
